name: Whirlwind-Colossus
description: Whirlwind-Colossus is among the largest gas giants ever surveyed, a world so massive it borders on brown dwarf classification. Its toxic atmosphere churns with whirlwind systems that stack vertically through dozens of cloud layers, creating columns of rotating gas that extend from the deepest observable depths to the uppermost atmospheric boundary. A thick ring of captured debris orbits the equator, the accumulated remnants of moons and asteroids ground to dust by tidal forces.

The planet radiates more heat than it receives from its star, a remnant of gravitational compression that keeps the deep atmosphere in a state of perpetual convection. The magnetic field is extraordinarily powerful, generating radiation belts that would be lethal to unshielded organisms at orbital distances. The whirlwind columns glow with chemical luminescence deep in the atmosphere, visible through gaps in the upper cloud deck as pillars of sickly green and pale orange light.

At a specific point in the upper atmosphere, instruments consistently detect spatial anomalies consistent with wormhole remnants, areas where the fabric of space-time appears to have been stressed or torn. These anomalies are stable but unpredictable, occasionally producing bursts of exotic radiation that match no known physical process. Some theorists believe the planet's extreme mass and magnetic field may be naturally maintaining or preserving these remnants from some ancient event.

Whirlwind-Colossus is a paradox of resources and risk. Its antimatter traces and helium-3 reserves are staggering, but the radiation belts, extreme gravity, and spatial anomalies make harvesting operations dangerous even by gas-giant standards. The wormhole remnants represent either a monumental scientific discovery or a monumental hazard, depending on whether they can be stabilized, and the prospect of faster-than-light travel implications ensures that research funding never lacks for this hostile, fascinating giant.
